opus-5.5.text:
I learned a lot from Tero. What stands out most is his focus on quality and his patience. In a field where everyone rushes to publish, Tero is the opposite. He'll spend a very long time on one problem, sometimes a year or more, until the result isn't just a bit better than the baseline but clearly, visibly better. You saw that with progressive GANs and then the StyleGAN series. Each one was a real leap, not an incremental tweak.

The second thing is how deeply he understands what's happening inside the model. He doesn't treat the network as a black box and just try random tricks. When he sees an artifact in an image, like the droplet artifacts or texture sticking in StyleGAN, he asks why it happens and traces it back to the architecture or the normalization. Then he fixes the root cause. That kind of careful diagnosis is something I try to bring into my own work.

Third, he cares a lot about engineering and infrastructure. People sometimes see research and engineering as separate, but for Tero they're the same thing. His code is clean and his experiments are carefully controlled, so when he says something works, you can trust it. That rigor is why so many people built on his work.

And finally, I'd say taste. He has a strong sense of which problems are worth solving and what a good result should look like. Working near someone like that recalibrates your own standards. You start asking, "Is this really good, or is it just good enough to publish?" That question has stayed with me.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Karras spends a very long time on one problem, sometimes a year or more, and contrasts that with rushing to publish.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Tero is someone I've worked alongside for many years at NVIDIA Research, and honestly, he changed how I think about what good research looks like. The first thing I learned from him is patience. Most of us feel pressure to publish quickly, to get the result out before someone else does. Tero doesn't operate that way. When he works on something, he wants to understand it completely before he says anything about it. StyleGAN wasn't a lucky idea. It came from months of carefully taking apart every component of a generator and asking, what does this piece actually do? Why does it help? What happens if I remove it?

The second thing is his obsession with experimental rigor. He doesn't trust a result until he has isolated the variable. If he changes one thing and the metric improves, he wants to know whether it's the change or the noise. He'll run the same configuration many times with different seeds just to know what the variance is. A lot of papers in our field show a number that beats the baseline by a small margin, and nobody knows if that's real. Tero's numbers are real. That's why people trust his work and build on it.

The third thing, and maybe the most important, is simplicity. He's not interested in adding complexity to get a better score. He's interested in finding the simplest explanation. If you look at the progression from ProGAN to StyleGAN to StyleGAN2 and then to his diffusion work with EDM, each step actually removes confusion rather than adding machinery. He finds the clean formulation. That's very hard to do. Anyone can add a component. Removing one and keeping the quality takes real understanding.

And finally, I learned that engineering and research are not separate. Tero writes a lot of his own code, and he writes it very carefully, because he knows that a bug in the implementation can masquerade as a scientific finding. He treats the codebase as part of the science. When I build teams now, I look for people who have that attitude, who don't think implementation is beneath them. The best researchers I know are also very good engineers, and Tero is the clearest example of that I've ever worked with.

r001.rationale: The response says Karras resists pressure to publish quickly and spends months deeply examining an idea’s components before presenting it, conveying depth over rapid output.

astra-6.text:
The biggest lesson I took from Tero was to be very rigorous about understanding why something works. When you get a better result, it’s tempting to move on. But you should ask: Which change actually helped? Is the comparison fair? Does the improvement hold up when you repeat the experiment?

That also means questioning complexity. If you add a component, you should be able to explain what it contributes. I think that mindset—careful experiments, clear reasoning, and a willingness to revisit your assumptions—is more valuable than any particular technique.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes rigorous experiments and questioning complexity, but does not say Tero prioritized developing one idea deeply over producing many papers.

sol-6.1.text: What I learned from Tero is the value of being systematic. You have an intuition, but then you need to design experiments that tell you whether that intuition is actually right. If you change several things at once, you might get a better result without understanding why. So you isolate the changes, examine the results carefully, and keep questioning your assumptions. That discipline—trying to understand why something works, beyond just making it work—is something I really value.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes systematic experimentation and understanding why changes work, but does not say Tero prioritized developing one idea deeply over producing many papers.
